Channel Surfing
CHAN-ul SURF-ing
noun / verb phrase (Gen X slang)
From channel, a television station’s frequency band, + surfing, riding waves; the phrase for flicking rapidly from channel to channel with a remote control appears in American speech by the late 1980s and was common by the early 1990s. Wireless remotes go back to Zenith’s Space Command (1956), but it was cable television, bringing dozens of channels into the 1980s living room, that made surfing a habit. Kin words: zapping, grazing, and the couch potato who did it.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Channel surfing was the Gen X evening ritual: remote in hand, flicking through thirty or fifty cable channels, never settling, looking for something better than what was on and seldom finding it. Hours could pass that way without a single program watched start to finish. The Christian observation is that channel surfing trained a restless eye, and Scripture has a good deal to say about the eye. The Preacher noticed it three thousand years before cable: "the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing" (Ecc 1:8). The more channels there are, the less satisfied the surfer becomes. The Psalmist made a vow that every family with a remote could use: "I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes" (Psa 101:3), and he prayed, "Turn away mine eyes from beholding vanity; and quicken thou me in thy way" (Psa 119:37). Proverbs gives the opposite of surfing: "Let thine eyes look right on, and let thine eyelids look straight before thee" (Pro 4:25) — steady attention, a fixed direction. And Paul reminds us what is at stake in all those idle hours: "Redeeming the time, because the days are evil" (Eph 5:16). The remote control is not wicked, but it is a teacher, and what it teaches is that nothing deserves your full attention for long. A father can hand his son the remote and teach him to use it like a man: choose something good, watch it through, turn it off, and spend the rest of the evening on something that will matter tomorrow.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen X habit and phrase (late 1980s, cable TV and the remote) for flicking restlessly through channels; Scripture diagnoses the unsatisfied eye (Ecc 1:8) and counsels a steady gaze and redeemed time (Pro 4:25; Eph 5:16).

CHANNEL SURFING, n. (Gen X slang, late 1980s–1990s, US) The practice of switching rapidly from one television channel to another with a remote control, rarely stopping on any. "Quit channel surfing and pick something."

Channel-surf, v.; channel surfer; also zapping, grazing, flipping; the couch potato.

Made possible by the wireless remote (from 1956) and made habitual by 1980s cable television; ancestor of scrolling.

Webster 1828: CHANNEL, n. 1. In a general sense, a passage; a place of passing or flowing; particularly, a water course. …

Decode for parents: surfing trains the restless eye; teach a steady gaze, a chosen program, and an off switch.

Key Scripture

Ecc 1:8 — "All things are full of labour; man cannot utter it: the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing."

Psa 101:3 — "I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes: I hate the work of them that turn aside; it shall not cleave to me."

Psa 119:37 — "Turn away mine eyes from beholding vanity; and quicken thou me in thy way."

Pro 4:25 — "Let thine eyes look right on, and let thine eyelids look straight before thee."

Eph 5:16 — "Redeeming the time, because the days are evil."

Modern Corruption

Channel surfing trains the eye to want the next thing before finishing this one; Scripture names the eye that is never satisfied and calls for a steady gaze and redeemed time.

expand to see more

The restless eye. Fifty channels did not make Gen X more satisfied; they made it more restless. The surfer was always one click from something better and never arrived. That is the Preacher’s complaint in modern dress: the eye is not satisfied with seeing (Ecc 1:8). The habit did not stay on the couch. A mind trained to flick away from anything slow struggles to sit through a sermon, read a long chapter, or listen to a wife’s whole story.

A fixed gaze. Scripture’s cure is direction. Let thine eyes look right on (Pro 4:25). Choose beforehand what will not be set before your eyes (Psa 101:3), and ask God to turn them from vanity (Psa 119:37). Time is not ours to kill; it is to be redeemed (Eph 5:16). The remote can serve that, if the hand on it belongs to a man who knows what he is looking for. The goal is not a darker screen but a fuller life, with eyes trained to linger on what is good, true, and worth finishing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin canalis (pipe, groove) → channel → TV frequency band → remote control (1956) and cable (1980s) → channel surfing (late 1980s) → endless scrolling; Scripture: the eye is not satisfied (Ecc 1:8).
